answer: The plan is honest and well-structured, but it reads as a concept description rather than a fundable case. Priorities for revision: (1) Quantify the market bottom-up. Replace 'tens of millions' and 'small fraction' with explicit math (e.g., regional adult population x % interested x realistic conversion x price; number of target schools x % with supply budgets x $90), and state a serviceable, obtainable first-year market. (2) Fix and show unit economics. Home Kit COGS of ~$11 plus $6-8 shipping against a $28 price leaves roughly $9-11 before any acquisition cost, and the subscription at $24 is thinner still. Provide a per-unit P&L, obtain at least two or three supplier quotes (even at 100-unit volume), and explore ways to cut shipping cost (smaller/lighter kit, regional delivery, local pickup). Model CAC explicitly, even as a range with assumptions, and show payback and contribution margin; subscription churn and refill attach rate should be assumptions you state and test. (3) Convert validation into evidence. Twelve home users and one class are a start, but 'generally said they felt more confident' is anecdotal. Report specifics: sample size, survey questions, % who completed a batch successfully, % who would buy, willingness-to-pay test results (e.g., pre-orders, a priced waitlist, or a pilot sale at $28), and teacher intent to purchase. Even 20-30 pre-sales or letters of intent would materially strengthen the case. (4) Sharpen the competitive position and defensibility. Name specific competitors and prices, show a comparison table, and explain why a safety-and-confidence focus is a durable edge. Consider what is protectable (photo reference library, validated pH-checkpoint protocol, curriculum alignment, teacher relationships, brand trust) and how you would build it. (5) Address safety and liability as a core issue, not a line item. For a food-safety product, the pH-strip 'safe to eat' rule is also your largest legal exposure. Explain how the protocol was validated (lab testing, expert review), what regulations apply to selling kits with salt and food guidance (and to school purchases), and how the $3,000 legal/insurance/food-safety line will be scoped. Seeking an advisor in food regulation or CPG now, and naming one before submission, would close the gap you already identify. (6) Decide on focus or justify the dual market. Home and classroom have different buyers, sales cycles (school budget calendars, procurement rules), price points, and channels. Either present a sequenced plan with rationale for which goes first, or show that the shared core product genuinely lowers cost; reconsider whether the $90 classroom kit for 30 students (about $3 each) is viable given materials and the jar cost per group. (7) Strengthen the ask. Tie the $10,000 to measurable milestones and a decision framework (e.g., sell 100 Home Kits at full price within 90 days, 10 paying classrooms, a CAC under a target, repeat rate over a target), and show how the runway reaches the learning goals. Provide the arithmetic that 100 Home + 20 Classroom kits fits within $4,000 (about $33/unit all-in leaves little margin for error). Clarify what happens after the grant (path to a break-even volume or next funding). (8) Show traction beyond the prototype. Build the simplest landing page and email waitlist before submission, a few testimonials with permission, photos of the kit and user batches, and a short timeline of the next six months. Even a tiny pre-order test demonstrates demand better than any estimate. (9) Tighten presentation. Lead with a one-sentence value proposition and a crisp traction/ask summary; cut hedging language ('we hope,' 'we believe,' 'we assume') in favor of stated assumptions plus how you will validate them; add a short risks-and-mitigations section (safety incident, supplier cost, seasonality, low subscription retention); and include a brief founder commitment statement (time, full vs. part-time) given the team are current students.
